The family council

Sunday 6 June 2037, at Gérard’s café, at the bottom of rue d’Austerlitz. Madame Roux, 91, wants to take Farid in, in the spare room of her flat in Villeurbanne. Her son Philippe, who has come from Paris, is against it. Inès, who wants to become a lawyer, defends the plan.
Mum, I understand your idea, but given your age, it’s far too risky.
I may be ninety-one, but I’m not a piece of furniture. It’s my flat, so it’s my decision.
You fell in April. If the neighbour hadn’t heard you, you’d have stayed on the floor all night.
Exactly. Since your mother lives alone, someone being there at night would protect her. That’s why this plan is a solution, not a risk.
Granted, but we don’t know this boy. In case there were a problem, who would be responsible?
An association signs an agreement with the three of you. On the other hand, if your mother goes into a care home against her will, she risks losing the will to live.
Farid starts nursing school in September. He knows first-aid procedures, whereas you live four hundred kilometres away.
That’s not fair, Mum. I come whenever I can.
I know, darling. Although you come often, the evenings are long. For lack of company, I talk to the radio.
We’re not asking you to say yes right away. We’re proposing a one-month trial, provided that everything is in writing.
One month… And unless everything goes perfectly, you’ll come to Paris?
If it doesn’t work, I’ll think about it. But if it works, you’ll come and eat Farid’s palaw. So you have nothing to lose.
(he sighs) You’ve always won every debate, Mum. All right, one month.

“Pwees-kuh”: “ui” is said in one breath, a short “u” gliding into “i”.
“Nay-ahn-mwan”: two nasals, “an” and “oin”; the final “s” is silent.

1. Cause: why?
French has several connectors of cause, each with its own nuance:
neutral cause, answers “pourquoi ?”
Je reste parce qu’il pleut.
a cause both people already know
Puisque tu es là, aide-moi.
a cause placed at the start of the sentence
étant donné que / vu que
a cause stated as an established fact (careful register)
Étant donné ton âge, c’est risqué.
à cause de + noun
NEGATIVE or neutral cause
À cause de la pluie, le match est annulé.
faute de + noun/infinitive
the cause is a lack of something
Faute de temps, je n’ai pas fini.

Typical mistakes: causal “comme” goes at the START of the sentence (“Je reste comme il pleut” ✗). “À cause de” with a good result sounds odd: “À cause de toi, j’ai réussi” ✗ → “Grâce à toi, j’ai réussi” ✓.
2. Consequence: and so?
It’s my flat, so it’s my decision.
She lives alone, that’s why someone being there would protect her.
You have nothing to lose. Therefore, say yes.
She was so tired that she fell asleep.
There were so many people that we left.
“Si bien que” and “de sorte que” take the INDICATIVE when they express a real result. “Tellement / si + adjective + que”, “tant de / tellement de + noun + que”.
3. Concession: although…
A concession acknowledges the other person’s argument but declares it insufficient. It is the heart of every B2 debate.
+ SUBJUNCTIVE
Bien que tu viennes souvent, les soirées sont longues.
+ INDICATIVE
Même si tu viens souvent, les soirées sont longues.
Malgré son âge, elle est autonome.
J’ai beau avoir 91 ans, je ne suis pas un meuble.
certes…, mais
two clauses
Certes, il est jeune, mais il est responsable.
pourtant / néanmoins / cependant
at the start of the second clause
Il est jeune. Néanmoins, il est responsable.
Trap: “même si” is NOT used with the subjunctive, nor with the conditional: “Même si il serait…” ✗ → “Même s’il est…” ✓. Watch the elision too: “même s’il”, but “même si elle”.
4. Contrast: on the one hand, on the other
Contrast sets two facts side by side without one cancelling the other:
Farid knows first aid, whereas you live far away.
Philippe is cautious, while his mother loves taking risks.
The plan has risks. On the other hand, it has many advantages.
Instead of going into a care home, she stays at home.
“Par contre” means the same as “en revanche” but is more informal. In the exam and in writing, prefer “en revanche”.

“Au cas où” is the only connector of condition followed by the CONDITIONAL. “Au cas où il pleuvra” ✗ → “Au cas où il pleuvrait” ✓.

La chambre du fond

In the spring of 2037, Farid had a problem he hadn’t told anyone about. For three years he had been living in a hostel for young adults in Villeurbanne, with thirty other boys from all over the world. The hostel was noisy, the kitchen was dirty and the showers were cold, but it was a roof. However, his contract ended on his twenty-first birthday, 21 August. After that date he would have to leave. And on 1 September he was starting nursing school. He had no flat, no guarantor and no family in France. All he had was a place at a school, a small round stone in his pocket and a lot of courage.

He had started looking in March. Amina, who couldn’t see a problem without opening a spreadsheet, had helped him write everything down. By early June the spreadsheet listed sixty-three ads, forty-one messages sent, four viewings and zero positive answers. The reasons were always the same, even if no one ever said them plainly. He had no guarantor. He had no employment contract. He had a foreign first name. One landlady had told him on the phone that she preferred to rent to “a serious female student, with parents”. Farid had answered politely that he was serious, and that he too had had parents.

He didn’t talk about it to the others, because he was ashamed. Everyone had already helped him so much since the exam in December. Bertrand had lent him a coat, Gérard gave him free tea, Ioana invited him to dinner every Sunday. He didn’t want to become, as he put it, “the boy with problems”. But Rose-Hélène, who was nine and had eyes that saw everything, had noticed that he no longer smiled when she played him the three notes on her harmonica. One Thursday she had asked him if he was ill. He had said no. She had answered, very seriously, that grown-ups were bad liars and that she would keep an eye on him.

In the end, it wasn’t Rose-Hélène who discovered the secret. It was Madame Roux. One Thursday in May, during the orchestra’s break, Farid was on the phone in the corridor with an estate agency. He was speaking quietly, but Madame Roux, who was sitting on her chair by the door, had sharper ears than people thought. She heard everything. The guarantor, the hostel, 21 August, and the voice of the woman from the agency saying she was sorry but that, under the circumstances, she couldn’t do anything. Farid hung up. He stood for a minute with his forehead against the wall. Then he went back into the hall and picked up his foghorn again, as if nothing had happened.

Simone Roux was ninety-one. For sixty-two years she had lived in the same flat in Villeurbanne, on the fifth floor of a building in the Gratte-Ciel district, with a lift that broke down once a month and a balcony from which you could see the two towers of the town hall. The flat had four rooms. There was the kitchen, where she spent her days. There was the living room, with the radio, her husband’s clarinet in a glass cabinet and the photos from the Saturday dances. There was her bedroom. And there was the back room, her son Philippe’s, where no one had slept since 1992.

Her husband, Lucien, had died in 2019. For forty years they had both played in a dance band, “Les Copains du Samedi”, he on the clarinet, she on the saxophone, then on the clarinet too, once she had decided she played better than he did. They had kept three generations of Villeurbanne people dancing, in village halls, at weddings and at the Bastille Day dances. Since Lucien’s death, Simone only played with the Thursday orchestra, where she sat at the back of the hall and beat time with her walking stick, always a little ahead, because, she said, at her age you don’t have time to wait for the beat.

In April she had fallen in her kitchen, at two in the morning, on her way to get a glass of water. Nothing was broken, but she hadn’t managed to get up. She had stayed on the floor for an hour, calling for help in a weaker and weaker voice, until her downstairs neighbour, Madame Benali, heard her through the ceiling and came up with the spare key. Philippe had arrived from Paris the next day. He was sixty-three, an engineer with the SNCF, and he had always been convinced that his mother was going to do something foolish. This time he had proof.

He had brought three care-home brochures. He had put them on the kitchen table, next to the sugar tin. Simone had looked at them without touching them. There were photos of gardens, of bright dining rooms, of smiling old ladies playing cards. Simone had said she didn’t like cards and had never in her life seen old ladies that smiling. Philippe had said she could no longer live alone. Simone had said she wasn’t alone, she had her radio. Philippe had closed his eyes, just as he used to when he was twelve and she refused to buy a television.

It was in the newspaper that Simone had found the idea. One morning in May, in Le Progrès, she had read an article about intergenerational home-sharing. A Lyon association, “Toit Partagé”, put older people with a spare room in touch with young people looking for somewhere to live. The young person paid a very modest rent. In exchange, they committed to being there in the evenings and at night, to sharing some meals and to doing small favours. They were neither a nurse nor a servant. They were, the article said, “a presence”. Simone had cut out the article with her dressmaker’s scissors and put it in her purse.

On the Thursday she overheard Farid on the phone, she took the article out of her purse during the second half of the rehearsal and read it three times. After the rehearsal, while everyone was putting away the music stands, she signalled to Farid to come over. He came, as always, to carry her chair to the taxi. She told him to sit down. He sat down. She handed him the article. He read it slowly, moving his lips a little, as he still did with difficult texts. Then he looked up at her, without understanding.

“I have a spare room,” said Simone. “It’s at the end of the corridor. It looks onto the courtyard, so it’s quiet. There’s a bed, a desk and some football posters from 1985 that you’re allowed to take down.” Farid blushed to the tips of his ears. He said he couldn’t accept. He said she didn’t know him. Simone answered that she had known him since January, that he carried her chair every Thursday, that he said hello to the taxi driver and that he had never once missed the fifth bar of the silence. In her view, that was more than she knew about most people.

Farid asked for a few days to think about it. He spent three sleepless nights in his hostel bed, listening to his neighbour’s snoring and the noise of the cars on the boulevard. He was afraid of being a nuisance. He was afraid he wouldn’t know how to live in someone’s home, after three years in a hostel and a year on the road. Above all, he was afraid of growing attached to an old lady and losing her, the way he had lost everything else. On the fourth day he called Simone. He said yes. Simone said: “Very good. Now we have to convince my son. That’s another matter.”

Philippe took the news very badly. On the phone, he first thought his mother was joking. Then he shouted. He said she knew nothing about this boy, that you read terrible stories in the papers, that swindlers liked lonely old ladies, and that she didn’t realise. Simone listened without interrupting. When he had finished, she said: “Have you finished, darling? Good. Then come on Sunday. We’ll talk about it at the café, with Farid, with the people who know him, and you can ask him all the questions you like.” Philippe said he would come, but only to say no to her face.

When the news spread, the whole gang mobilised, and Inès took charge. She was eighteen, had just passed her baccalauréat and was starting at the Lyon 3 law faculty in September. She had wanted to be a lawyer since the age of twelve. She declared that this would be her first case. She prepared for Sunday as if for a court hearing. She asked Amina for figures on loneliness among older people. She asked Bertrand for a letter of recommendation, on official paper. She asked Hortense Valmont for an article about home-sharing. And she asked Farid not to speak unless someone asked him a question.

She spent Saturday evening at Julien and Ioana’s, on rue d’Austerlitz, rehearsing her arguments in front of a tough audience: Rose-Hélène and Henri-Ion. Rose-Hélène played Philippe. She crossed her arms, frowned and said “No” to every sentence, in a deep voice. Henri-Ion played the judge, with a wooden spoon for a gavel. Inès learnt a lot that evening. She learnt that an argument that is too long puts the judge to sleep. She learnt that it is better to acknowledge your opponent’s good arguments before fighting them. And she learnt that a six-year-old judge can be bought with a biscuit.

On Sunday 6 June, at ten o’clock, everyone was at Gérard’s café, at the bottom of rue d’Austerlitz. Philippe arrived from Part-Dieu station by taxi, a newspaper under his arm, looking like a man who had come to sign a divorce. He kissed his mother, shook Farid’s hand without looking at him, and sat down opposite Inès, who had spread out three coloured folders in front of her. Gérard brought the coffees without being asked. At the counter, the op-ed club pretended to read the papers. In reality, nobody was turning the pages.

The debate lasted two hours. Philippe began with the argument of age. Inès replied with the argument of presence. Philippe talked about the fall in April. Inès pointed out that if someone had been sleeping in the back room that night, Madame Roux wouldn’t have spent an hour on the tiles. Philippe said that nobody knew this boy. Inès took out Bertrand’s letter, which began with “Sir” and ended with “the expression of my highest consideration”, and which said, in between, that Farid was the most reliable person he had met since leaving the Court of Audit.

Then Amina presented her figures. According to a study she had found, one in four people over eighty spent their days without speaking to anyone. She added, looking at her spreadsheet, that older people who lived with someone fell less often, because they moved around more. Philippe listened with his arms crossed, exactly like Rose-Hélène the evening before. Then he said, with a little smile, that you can make figures say anything. Amina looked at him over her glasses and replied that this was true, but only when you can’t count.

The op-ed club almost applauded. Gérard stopped them with a look. Philippe changed strategy. He had kept his strongest argument for the end. Turning at last directly to Farid, he said the problem wasn’t today. The problem was tomorrow. “Let’s suppose it works,” he said. “My mother gets used to you. She waits for you in the evening. She bakes you cakes. And then one day you find a flat, a girlfriend, a job in Marseille, and you leave. That will be normal, you’re twenty. But she’ll be even lonelier than before. What do you say to that?”

There was a silence. Inès opened her mouth to answer, but Farid put his hand on her arm. It was the first time he had spoken since the start. He said, slowly, in his still slightly hesitant French: “You’re right, sir. It’s a real argument. I can’t promise you the future. Nobody can. But I can tell you one thing. When I left my village, I couldn’t say goodbye to my grandmother. She was asleep. My mother told me not to wake her, because she would have cried and I might have changed my mind. I think about that every day.”

“So all I promise you is this,” Farid went on. “If I leave one day, I won’t leave while she’s asleep. I’ll leave saying goodbye, leaving her my address, and I’ll come back on Sundays, unless she asks me not to come any more. And she won’t be alone, because now she has all these people.” With a gesture he pointed to the café, to Inès, Amina, Gérard, and the op-ed club, who were no longer even pretending to read. Philippe looked around. He looked at his mother. Simone said nothing. Her eyes were wet, and she was smiling.

Philippe sighed. He said he would accept a one-month trial, in July, and not a day more without thinking it over. He added that if anything went wrong, even a detail, he would come and fetch his mother himself. Inès put away her three folders with the dignity of a lawyer who has just won a case she thought was lost. Gérard offered croissants all round. And the old Latin teacher from the op-ed club declared, raising his cup, that it was the finest plea he had heard since Cicero, which, according to Bertrand, wasn’t quite accurate, but was still a very fine compliment.

The following Tuesday, the association’s adviser, Madame Ferrand, came to the flat in Gratte-Ciel. She was a woman of about fifty, calm and precise, who had set up more than two hundred home-shares. She inspected the back room, checked the lock, talked for a long time with Simone, then alone with Farid. She explained the rules. The rent would be fifty euros a month. Farid would be at home five evenings a week and every night, except for exceptions announced in advance. He would replace neither a doctor nor a care assistant. And each of them would have the right, at any time, to end the trial without having to give a reason.

On Thursday 1 July, Farid moved in. He didn’t have many things: a big sports bag, three library books, his French exercise books, a green plant Haruka had given him and a small red plastic harmonica. Bernard Delorme had insisted on coming with his van, although a sports bag fitted perfectly well on a tram. Rose-Hélène had come too, with a drawing she had made to decorate the room: a lime tree, an old lady with a clarinet and a boy with a foghorn, all three playing, with musical notes flying off towards a far too big sun.

The back room hadn’t changed since 1992. There was a narrow bed with a tartan blanket, a school desk, a model plane hanging from the ceiling on fishing line and, on the walls, posters of a football team whose players nobody remembered any more. Farid asked if he could keep the plane. Simone said he could keep everything or take everything down, that it was his room now. Farid kept the plane and the posters. He only added Rose-Hélène’s drawing above the bed, and put his small round stone on the desk, next to the lamp.

The first days were a little awkward. They didn’t yet know how to live together. Farid got up at half past five, out of habit, and tiptoed so as not to wake Simone, who had been up since five and was waiting for him in the kitchen, wondering why he was hiding. Simone talked a lot, Farid very little. On the second evening she taped a list of rules to the fridge, handwritten in big slanting letters. Farid read it while drinking his tea. He laughed for the first time since he had arrived. It was, he said later, the best lesson in logical connectors of his life.

The list said: “Rule number one: since we both get up early, we’ll have breakfast together. Rule number two: you may play music, provided it isn’t rap after ten p.m. Rule number three: although I’m old, I’m not deaf, so there’s no need to shout. Rule number four: in case I don’t answer when you knock on my door, come in. Rule number five: Lucien’s clarinet is not to be touched, unless I give it to you myself. Rule number six: we don’t talk about care homes in this home.”

Farid learnt fast. He learnt that Simone drank her coffee from a bowl, never a cup, and dunked a slice of bread with salted butter in it, because Lucien was Breton on his mother’s side. He learnt that the radio stayed on all day, on a station that played songs from the sixties, and that she sang along, always out of tune but always to the end. Simone, for her part, learnt that Farid didn’t eat pork, that he read late at night with a torch so as not to waste electricity, and that he folded his clothes with military precision. She told him that here the electricity was included in the fifty euros.

On the first Sunday, Farid cooked. He made a qabuli palaw, the festive dish of his country: rice scented with cardamom and cumin, lamb, carrots cut into thin strips, and raisins. He spent three hours in the kitchen. Simone watched him from her chair, commenting on everything. She said it was far too spicy from the very first mouthful. Then she had a second plate. Then a third. The following Sunday, in return, she taught him her own mother’s gratin dauphinois, with garlic, lots of cream and infinite patience. Farid thought it lacked spices. He had three helpings.

In the evenings, instead of listening to the radio, they talked. Or rather, at first, Simone talked and Farid listened. She told him about the Saturday dances, the weddings where they played until five in the morning, the newlyweds who quarrelled during the slow dance, and the evening in 1968 when the band played through a power cut, by the light of cigarette lighters, without anyone stopping dancing. One evening, despite rule number five, she took Lucien’s clarinet out of the glass cabinet and tried to teach him to play it. Farid blew with all his might. All that came out was a kettle’s whistle. Simone laughed so hard she had to sit down.

Philippe phoned every evening at eight o’clock sharp. He always asked the same thing: “Is everything all right, Mum?” And Simone always answered, cheerfully: “He hasn’t murdered me yet, darling.” Philippe didn’t find that funny. After a week he started asking to speak to Farid too. Their conversations were short and polite. Philippe asked whether his mother was taking her medication, whether she was drinking enough water in the heat, whether she used her stick in the flat. Farid answered precisely, like a report. Yes. Yes, a litre and a half. No, but he was working on it. Philippe hung up saying “Thank you”, and that was all.

One evening in the second week, Simone showed Farid the photo album from the dances. There was Lucien, young, with a moustache and a flowery shirt. There was Simone at thirty, in a red dress, a saxophone in her arms. There were village halls full of people dancing. Farid turned the pages in silence. Then Simone asked, gently, without looking at him: “And your father, what did he do?” Farid didn’t answer right away. He closed the album. He looked for a long time at the clarinet in the cabinet. Then he said: “My father was a musician. Like you.”

His name was Daoud. He played the rubab, a long-necked Afghan lute with a body carved from a single piece of mulberry wood and a skin stretched over it, like a drum. He played at weddings in the valley, and sometimes as far as Herat, the big city, where he was well known. Farid remembered his father sitting in the courtyard in the evening, the instrument on his knees, surrounded by neighbours. He remembered the smell of tea and smoke, and the children falling asleep against their mothers while the music rose towards the mountains. His father used to say that a rubab was a heart you held in your arms.

Then, when Farid was four, music had been banned. Instruments were smashed in public squares. Musicians had to fall silent or leave. Daoud hadn’t wanted to leave, because his mother was too old to travel. He hadn’t wanted to fall silent either. So he had hidden his rubab in the wall of the house, behind a carpet, in a hole he had dug himself. And on some nights, when the whole village was asleep, he took it out. He played so softly, Farid said, that you had to hold your breath to hear it. The whole family held its breath. For Farid, that was the sound of his childhood: an almost silent music.

For twelve years nobody had found out. Then, one autumn evening in 2033, someone had talked. Men had come. They had torn down the carpet, found the hole in the wall and taken out the rubab. They had smashed it in the courtyard, in front of the whole family, with rifle butts. Then they had taken Daoud away. Farid was sixteen. His father never came back. No one ever found out where he was. Farid told all this in a flat voice, without crying, looking at the kitchen table. Simone said nothing. She just put her wrinkled hand on Farid’s hand and left it there.

A few months later, Farid’s mother had sold her jewellery, the jewellery from her wedding, to pay a smuggler. She was afraid they would come for her eldest son too. Farid had left one morning in February 2034, before dawn. He had taken a bag, a little money sewn into the lining of his jacket, and just one thing of his father’s: a small, round, smooth stone, picked up from the river behind the house. Daoud had given it to him when he was little, so that he could learn to tap out the rhythm on the table. He used to say it was a stone that counted time. Farid had kept it in his pocket for the whole journey. He still had it.

After a long while, Simone spoke in her turn. She said her maiden name was García. Her parents were Spanish. In February 1939, at the end of the Spanish Civil War, they had crossed the Pyrenees on foot, in the snow, with half a million other refugees. Her father carried his guitar on his back. The French gendarmes had taken it from him at the border, along with everything that looked like a weapon, and he never saw it again. Simone had been born in 1946 in Villeurbanne, into a family where Spanish was spoken at home and where, in the evening, they quietly sang songs that you weren’t supposed to sing too loudly.

“I’m a refugees’ daughter too,” said Simone. “My father bought another guitar in 1950, second-hand, with his first wages as a factory worker. He played it badly, because his fingers were ruined by the factory. But he played it every Sunday. He’s the one who taught me music.” She looked at Farid. “You see, you think you’ve lost music, and then it comes back by another road. My father lost his guitar at the border, and his daughter played the clarinet for sixty years.” Farid said he had never learnt to play the rubab. His father had wanted to teach him. They hadn’t had time.

That night Simone didn’t sleep. She thought until dawn. The next morning, while Farid was at the library, she phoned Thiébaut, the luthier in the Croix-Rousse, who had made a hundred and fifty-eight violins and had given one to Sorina for her wedding. She told him everything. Then she phoned Monsieur Haddad, who played the oud in the Thursday orchestra and knew the instruments of the East. She asked them whether it was possible to make a rubab, in one month, in Lyon. Thiébaut said he had never made one. Haddad said it was impossible. Simone replied that she hadn’t asked whether it was easy.

They needed mulberry wood. Thiébaut searched for a week. Then he remembered something all Lyon people forget: in the nineteenth century, Lyon was the capital of silk, and the canuts, the silk weavers of the Croix-Rousse, raised silkworms, which eat nothing but mulberry leaves. A few old mulberry trees were left in the courtyards on the slopes. One of them, in a courtyard on the Montée de la Grande-Côte, had been cut down the previous winter because it was in danger of falling. The wood was drying in a cellar. The owner, when he heard what it would be used for, didn’t want any money. He only asked to be invited on the day it was played.

Meanwhile, Simone played the spy. In the evenings she asked Farid to sing her his father’s songs, claiming she wanted to learn to play them on the clarinet. Farid sang softly, the way people sang in his family, with his eyes closed. Simone recorded everything on the phone Philippe had given her and which she had never used. She sent the recordings to Haddad, who listened to them ten times, worked out the chords and modes, and drew for Thiébaut the length of the neck, the number of strings and the position of the tuning pegs. Farid suspected nothing. He just thought Simone asked a lot of questions.

On the night of 19 July, it was thirty-four degrees in Lyon. It was a heatwave. The windows were open and the air didn’t move. At three in the morning, Farid was woken by a dull thud, followed by a moan. He leapt out of bed. The bathroom light was on. Simone was on the floor, between the bath and the washbasin, in her nightdress, her eyes open. She said: “Don’t panic. I think the tiles have got the better of me again.” She was trying to smile, but she was very pale and was holding her left hip with her hand.

Farid didn’t panic. In June he had taken the first-aid course required for entry to nursing school, and he remembered every word the instructor had said. Above all, don’t lift the person up. He asked her whether her head hurt, whether she could feel her legs, whether she could move her toes. He put a folded towel under her head and a light blanket over her legs. Then he called 15. He spoke slowly and clearly, as Inès had taught him for the DELF oral: “Woman, ninety-one years old. Fall in the bathroom. Conscious. Pain in the left hip. No loss of consciousness.”

The dispatching doctor asked him more questions, and Farid answered them all. Then he was told that an ambulance was on its way and that she must not be moved. Farid sat on the floor next to Simone, on the cold tiles, and took her hand. She was frightened now, and she no longer hid it. She said she didn’t want to go to hospital, because at her age you never knew if you’d come back. Farid didn’t know what to say. So he did the only thing he knew how to do. He whistled the eight bars of the waltz, very softly. Simone closed her eyes. Her hand relaxed in his.

The ambulance arrived in twelve minutes. The paramedics put Simone on a stretcher with a thousand precautions, and Farid rode with her. At the A&E of the Édouard-Herriot hospital it was crowded, because of the heat: dehydrated old people, crying children, a man who was singing. Farid waited in the corridor, on a plastic chair. At a quarter past four he called Philippe. He dreaded that call more than anything else. Philippe picked up on the second ring. Farid explained everything, in order, without forgetting anything. Philippe listened without interrupting. Then he said only: “I’m taking the first train.”

Around seven, a young doctor came to see Farid in the corridor. She said nothing of Simone’s was broken. She had a large bruise on her hip and was slightly dehydrated because of the heatwave, which probably explained the dizzy spell and the fall. They would keep her in for two days for observation. Then the doctor added something Farid never forgot: “Are you the one who found her? You did exactly the right things. If you had lifted her up, you could have made a fracture worse. Are you a nurse?” Farid said: “Not yet. In September.” The doctor smiled. “Then see you soon, colleague.”

Philippe arrived at the hospital at half past nine, still in his suit, a small suitcase in his hand. He had taken the six o’clock TGV. A nurse showed him to his mother’s room. He pushed the door open gently. Simone was awake, in bed, with a drip in her arm. And next to her, on a plastic chair too small for him, Farid was asleep, his head tilted onto his shoulder, still holding the old lady’s hand. Simone put a finger to her lips. “Shh,” she whispered. “He’s asleep. He didn’t sleep a wink all night.” Philippe stopped on the threshold.

He stayed there a long time without moving. He looked at his mother, who wouldn’t let go of the boy’s hand. He looked at the boy, who was sleeping like a child. Then he sat down on the other side of the bed, took his mother’s other hand, and said nothing. Later, Simone told Rose-Hélène that it was the first time in years that her son had sat next to her for more than ten minutes without looking at his watch or talking about care homes. She said she should have fallen sooner. Rose-Hélène answered, very seriously, that it wasn’t a good method.

When Farid woke up, Philippe invited him for a coffee at the hospital cafeteria. They sat face to face, in front of two paper cups. Philippe spoke first. He said he owed him an apology. He said he had been afraid ever since the fall in April, and that fear makes you unfair. Then he said: “Given what you did last night, I have no argument left.” Farid shook his head. “Yes, sir, you do. You have one. You’re her son. I’m not taking your place. I’m only looking after the back room until you come back on Sundays.”

Philippe stayed in Villeurbanne for a week. He slept on the living-room sofa, because he refused, very firmly, to take back the back room. With Farid, he put grab bars in the bathroom and a non-slip mat in front of the bath. They spent a whole afternoon arguing about the height of the bars, then realised they had both been wrong, and started again. On Sunday Philippe tasted the qabuli palaw. He said it was too spicy. Then he had two more helpings. Simone, from her armchair, said that it was clearly a family illness.

On 30 July, Madame Ferrand came back with the final agreement. All three of them signed it on the kitchen table, next to the sugar tin, in exactly the spot where Philippe had put his brochures in April. The agreement was valid for one year, renewable until the end of Farid’s studies. Before signing, Philippe asked if he could add a clause by hand. Madame Ferrand said it was unusual but possible. At the bottom of the last page, in his engineer’s handwriting, Philippe wrote: “Article 12: on Sundays, when I am in Lyon, we eat together. The cook is chosen by drawing lots.”

Thursday 5 August was the orchestra’s last rehearsal before the summer break. It was still very hot, and the Hélène Morel hall was full. Simone was there, on her chair, with her stick and her bruise, which had turned every colour of the rainbow. Philippe had stayed in Lyon an extra day for the occasion. The owner of the old mulberry tree from the Grande-Côte was sitting in the front row, a little shy. Farid couldn’t understand why there were so many people, nor why Rose-Hélène, beside him, was wriggling on her chair as if she had swallowed a secret too big for her.

After the waltz, Théo asked for silence. He said that tonight there was a present. Thiébaut stood up with a long, narrow case of pale wood that he had made himself. He said, in his gruff voice, that it was his hundred and fifty-ninth instrument, and the first that wasn’t a violin. He said it was made from the wood of a mulberry tree in the Croix-Rousse, which for a hundred and fifty years had fed the silk weavers’ silkworms, and that an instrument made of that wood was bound to have something to say. Then he handed the case to Farid. Farid opened it. And he was no longer able to say a single word.

It was a rubab. It wasn’t perfect. Haddad said a master from Kabul would have found fault with the neck, and Thiébaut said the skin would have needed six more months. But it was a rubab, with a body carved from a single piece of mulberry, a long neck and strings that shone under the lamps. Farid took it out of the case with both hands, very slowly, the way you carry a newborn baby. He set it on his knees, exactly like his father. He touched a string. The sound filled the hall, deep and soft. And the whole hall held its breath, without knowing that this was exactly the right thing to do.

Haddad helped him tune it. Then Farid began to play. He didn’t really know how to play. He played with what his hands remembered from the nights of his childhood, when his father sometimes placed his fingers on the strings, in secret. It was the song Daoud had played on the last night, before the men came: a wedding song from the valley, slow and joyful at the same time. Farid made a lot of mistakes. He started again. In the middle of the song, his hands stopped. He couldn’t remember what came next. He sat motionless, his eyes closed, his fingers on the strings, and silence fell over the hall.

Nobody moved. The whole orchestra knew that silence. They waited, as they waited every Thursday, without counting, but counting all the same. One bar. Two. Three. At the fifth, nobody sounded the foghorn, because Farid was the one who usually held it. So Rose-Hélène whistled three notes, very softly. Then Simone took out Lucien’s clarinet, which she had secretly brought in her big bag, and played three more notes, a little out of tune, but in their place. Farid opened his eyes again. His fingers found their way back. And he played his father’s song to the end.

When he had finished, the hall didn’t stand up to applaud right away. First there was a long silence, a real one, full and warm. Then Bernard Delorme sounded the foghorn, and everyone stood up at the same time. Holding the rubab against his chest, Farid said that his father used to say a rubab was a heart you held in your arms. He said that this heart had been smashed in 2033, in a courtyard, six thousand kilometres from here. And that a luthier, an oud player, a ninety-one-year-old clarinettist and an old mulberry tree from Lyon had just given it back to him.

On 21 August, for his twenty-first birthday, Simone threw a party in the flat in Gratte-Ciel. There were thirty of them in four rooms, which, according to Amina, made seven point five people per room. Madame Benali had brought almond crescents, Gérard a cold soup, Philippe a cake bought in Paris, which had travelled on the TGV on his knees. On 1 September, at seven in the morning, Farid set off for his first day at nursing school. Simone watched him go from the balcony, waving a tea towel. At the bottom of the street he turned round and whistled three notes. From the fifth floor, Simone answered.

That evening, when he got home, Farid found a new line on the list of rules stuck to the fridge. Simone had written it in red pen, at the bottom of the sheet, in her big slanting letters: “Rule number seven: since you’re here, I’m no longer afraid at night.” Farid stood in front of the fridge for a long time. Then he took the red pen and wrote underneath, in the careful handwriting of a pupil who minds his accents: “Rule number eight: since you’re here, neither am I.” The next morning, at breakfast, neither of them mentioned it. But Simone sang along with the radio, out of tune, and all the way to the end.

Reading text: Madame Roux’s letter

After the family council, Madame Roux wrote her son a letter to explain her decision at leisure. Underline all the connectors: cause, consequence, concession, contrast, condition. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Lettre de Madame Roux à son fils

My dear Philippe, since you left too quickly on Sunday, and since I speak better with a pen than on the phone, I’m writing to you. I’d like to explain my decision calmly, without a debate and without Inès, who talks faster than the two of us.

First of all, I know you’re afraid for me. That’s normal, and I thank you for it. Granted, I fell in April. Nevertheless, I got up again. If I go into a care home, I’ll be safe, that’s true. On the other hand, I won’t be at home any more, and I think that would kill me faster than a fall.

Next, you say we don’t know this boy. That’s not true. I’ve seen him every Thursday since January, at the orchestra. He carries my chair when I’m tired. He came to see me in hospital without anyone asking him to. Although he has lived through terrible things, he is gentle, patient and punctual, which is more than I can say for your father, God rest his soul.

Finally, this plan isn’t only good for me. For lack of housing, Farid will have to leave his hostel at the end of August, so he risks giving up his studies. However hard he looks, nobody wants to rent to a young refugee without a guarantor. I have four rooms and only one person to fill them.

So here is what I propose: a one-month trial, in July, with the association’s agreement. In case something went wrong, you could come whenever you like. Unless you find a real argument by then, we’ll sign at the end of the summer.

Lots of love, my boy. You have been a perfect son, whereas I was often an absent mother, because of the clarinet and the Saturday dances. Let me, for once, be an imperfect and happy old lady. Your mother, who loves you, Simone.
